speechtext:

Some veterans have had to wait more than a year to get their cases before the medical advisory branch. subsubtopic: IMPROVEMENT OF FACILITIES ON NATIVE RESERVES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Canadian government has announced its intention to provide Barbados with a $6.5 million loan to improve its water supply system so that 98 per cent of all households on that island can receive water service by 1985. While most Canadians should be proud of their ability to aid less fortunate countries in this way, they should also be aware that less than 50 per cent of the homes in native communities across Canada are properly serviced, and even where running water is available the quality is often so poor that it contributes significantly to the already appalling health conditions found on most reserves. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That this House condemn the government for its disgraceful lack of priority setting where native people are concerned and direct the government to act immediately to improve and upgrade housing and water services on Canada's native reserves, which are currently trailing well behind national standards.

The prospects of expansion in the Canadian mining industry are favourable if sufficient growth capital can be found and made available. As much of the growth capital is self-generated, the House welcomes the policy statement by the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) in an address to the Alberta chamber of resources recently in which she stated, and I quote: "Further, the government has no plan to increase the tax burden of the mineral sector at this time."

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday in the House the minister indicated, in response to a question from the hon. member for Athabasca, some willingness-and accordingly gave a ray of hope on the part of the federal government-to modify the government's rigid position with respect to the oil and gas pricing agreement and to certain provisions of the National Energy Program. At the same time, the colleague of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, was in the province of Alberta escalating further the confrontation and widening the rift by indulging in yet another vicious attack upon the industry in the province of Alberta, which I must say casts a rather bad reflection upon the sincerity of the minister and indeed of this government.
Since the Minister of Finance now seems to have opened the door somewhat, may I ask him, in the interests of all concerned and particularly in the interest of improving the atmosphere, if he would use his good influence in urging his colleague to refrain from using his traditional inflammatory tactics, and to establish a negotiating stance of common sense and practical reasoning so that negotiations can be renewed and an energy agreement concluded.

January 23, 1981
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext: I have not had a chance, Madam Speaker, to read all of the minister's statements in Alberta, but what I have read indicates that he is attempting to clarify some facts that have been obscured, that have not been fully understood. I do not find anything in his statements that is inflammatory. On the contrary, the minister has repeated the willingness of the Government of Canada to continue negotiations in good faith and has continuously invited the government of Alberta to enter into negotiations with the same outlook and the same attitude. That has always been the attitude of the Government of Canada.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there seems to be reluctance on the part of the federal government to initiate any new attempt to negotiate. Could the minister enlighten the House as to what progress has been made in terms of establishing a common set of numbers with respect to revenue sharing and supply projections inasmuch as that seems to be one of the basic and fundamental problems in terms of getting back to the negotiating table. For example, the federal government contends that Ottawa will not require any imports of oil by 1990, while the province of Alberta suggests we will be requiring some 734,000 barrels a day. In the area of revenue sharing, the federal government contends that the province's share is 43 per cent; the province contends it is 28 per cent. Has any progress been made in establishing a common set of numbers upon which the two levels of government can agree?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext: I do not think it will be possible to make very much progress in establishing a common data base until there is a readiness to have meetings of officials on a continuing basis at which these numbers could be examined. 1 agree with the hon. member that it ought to be possible and an effort should be undertaken to reach a common understanding of the facts, and that can be done only by a resumption, on a continuing basis, of discussions between officials of both governments.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext: The point must be made that it is the Government of Canada which has exercised unilateralism, so it should be the federal government which becomes the initiator in terms of getting back to the negotiating table. Canadians are finding it increasingly more difficult to understand the hypocrisy of the government. It is attacking an industry in one part of the country and bailing out industries in other parts of the country. When can we expect the government to act with some equality in terms of equal treatment for industries in all parts of the country?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am glad the hon. member raised the question of the negotiations. It is important to point out that after the Government of Canada released its energy plan and after the budget was delivered, the Prime Minister undertook and expressed a willingness to enter into negotiations with the Premier of Alberta. It is my understanding that at that time the premier was of the view discussions should take place initially between officials of both governments and that it was inappropriate to begin discussions between himself and the Prime Minister; that has been the situation up to the present time. I hope the hon. member's question will encourage all participants, especially the government of Alberta, to come forward more readily to have serious discussions on this problem.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEWAL OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH PRODUCING PROVINCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in view of what seems to be a rather conciliatory approach by the Minister of Finance, would he seize upon the opportunity to become more involved in the negotiating process? As long as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is engaged alone in dealing with the province of Alberta, the division will continue and there will be a further inflammation of the current rift. Will the Minister of Finance seize upon this opportunity to become personally involved in the negotiations?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not believe the issues involved between the Government of Canada and the producing provinces are matters of personality.

speechtext: I think they are.

speechtext: The minister might be surprised.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING OF POST-SECONDARY INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State. Under the federal government's established programs financial scheme, the government funnels some $3 billion to the provinces to help pay the operating costs of post-secondary institutions in the country. In light of the government's budget of October 28, which stated that the federal government intends to reduce substantially transfer payments to the provinces in areas under provincial jurisdiction, will the minister advise the House whether the government is planning to withdraw support for post-secondary education in Canada either by pulling out of established programs financing or reducing significantly the post-secondary education portion of that shared-cost program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Francis Fox (Secretary of State and Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING OF POST-SECONDARY INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would just add one element to the hon. member's preamble. While it is true that over $3 billion per year is transferred to the provinces for the purpose of post-secondary education, I would like to add that there is also the transfer of tax points which amount to approximately $1 billion and which bring the total federal contribution to post-secondary education to $4 billion.
Of course, we are quite aware of the importance of federal contributions to post-secondary education in Canada. We are committed to seeing an excellent post-secondary education program continue in Canada, but, as in other areas, we are interested in seeing improvements made in the way federal funds are spent.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING OF POST-SECONDARY INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Secretary of State; he did not answer my previous question. Since support for post-secondary education under established programs funding is designed in large part to equalize educational opportunities across the country, does the minister realize that any major withdrawal of that support would devastate the quality of university education, especially in my own region of the Atlantic provinces, that it would cause student fees to skyrocket throughout the country, that it would
cripple the economies of university towns and, in fact, would undermine the government's own commitment to increase substantially research and development in the country?
In light of those facts, will the government launch a joint federal-provincial inquiry, review or perhaps even a royal commission to investigate university financing before it makes significant changes to this important area of our public life?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING OF POST-SECONDARY INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I fully agree with the hon. member that federal involvement in post-secondary education in this country has been essential to the development of our excellent educational system. I also indicated that it was in the best interest of both sides of this House to see that funds be expended as efficiently as possible. Perhaps I could draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that on Tuesday next I shall be meeting with the provincial ministers of education and that we will probably touch upon this subject. Also there is no doubt that this matter is of great interest to the academic as well as the political community throughout Canada. An important seminar is to be held at Simon Fraser University on February 12 and 13 and it will bring together representatives of the academic community. My officials and I intend to be in attendance and we shall of course see that federal funds are spent as wisely as possible and that federal objectives are being met.

speechtext:

January 23, 1981

were greatly delayed in the Gaspe peninsula offices. subsubtopic: CN EXPRESS OFFICES-PROPOSED MEETING OF PRESIDENT WITH MINISTER
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. During the course of questioning at yesterday's Standing Committee on Transport, CN President Dr. R. A. Bandeen informed committee members that he had proposals for the transport minister regarding the retention of CN Express offices in Charlottetown and other maritime centres. He advised me that he will be requesting a meeting with the Minister of Transport some day next week to present his proposals for the minister's consideration. In view of the urgency of the situation, that being that some CN employees have already received their notices of lay-off, will the minister assure this House that he will do everything possible to allow Dr. Bandeen to meet and present his proposals for the maintenance of CN Express offices in Charlottetown and other maritime centres?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has described the situation very well. Dr. Bandeen is going to tell me the results of his review of that situation next week. Prime Minister tell the House, in light of the two reports which were tabled in the House in July and December by the
January 23, 1981

parliamentary task forces on North-South relations, whether the government is now reviewing its public assistance policies and whether we can expect that in the near future the government will make a statement on the revision of those policies so as to ensure that people will show renewed interest in the Prime Minister's personal endeavour as regards the North-South dialogue?

subtopic: NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS INQUIRY WHETHER NEW POLICY WILL BE ANNOUNCED

subsubtopic: LACK OF FACILITIES IN NORTHWEST NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Although I would like once again to draw his attention to the problem of railway services in my riding, this morning my question relates to transport services generally. I would like to ask him whether his department or the Canadian Transport Commission are planning an early review of the full question of regional transportation within the Atlantic area. I ask this while emphasizing particularly the shortcomings in air services in northwestern New Brunswick, the region I represent in the House, of course.

subsubtopic: LACK OF FACILITIES IN NORTHWEST NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are two comments I can make on that subject. First, we are making a general review of VIA operations. Two or three years after setting up the corporation the government feels the need for reflection and that will lead to discussions with specialized groups, and with hon. members of course.
Second, several weeks ago I began an exchange of views with the transport ministers of the Atlantic provinces, including Newfoundland, on a concept whereby we would make up an envelope which would enable the provinces, in conjunction with the federal government, to adopt what I feel would be a much more constructive, much more effective and much more intelligent approach to transportation in those provinces. For instance, we might end up by saving money on certain means of transportation and those savings could then be invested in other modes of transportation. It is with that background in mind that some day I would like to reply at length to the hon. member's question.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. 1 will be very brief. In the oral question period I posed two questions to the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) concerning the established programs financing scheme. In reply to my questions 1 believe the minister might inadvertently have misled the House. He probably would not want that misleading information on the public record.
In my preamble I said that under the established programs financing scheme, $3 billion is funnelled to the provinces to help them pay the operating costs of post-secondary education institutions. In his reply to my questions the Secretary of State said that established programs financing included federal funds to provinces through cash payments and through tax points and that I perhaps had not included the tax points in my own calculation of $3 billion. 1 might refer the minister and the House to the Government of Canada's own statement of financial operations for the fiscal year 1980-81, of November, 1980.
That statement makes it clear that the $3 billion figure I quoted includes both cash payments, amounting to a total of about SI.6 billion, and tax points, totalling about $1.4 billion. That is for the fiscal year 1980-81. I am sure that the Secretary of State would not want to leave those figures he quoted on the public record because they are clearly wrong. The figure is not $4 billion but, rather, $3 billion.

demeans every member in this House in the eyes of the free world. It affects every member's relations with the United States of America, and particularly with the new administration. The statement I quoted this morning during question period was as follows:
At least they didn't bring in the CIA like they have in other foreign countries.
I feel that that statement made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) clearly reflects on every member of this House with respect to relations with the countries of the free world, particularly the United States. He said: Madam Speaker, the bill before us on second reading this afternoon-which may be referred to in short as the Customs Tariff Act-proposes a large number of amendments to the Customs Tariff, which the government introduced in three separate notices of ways and means motions. Most amendments in the bill relate to the tariff concessions Canada agreed to in the Tokyo Round trade negotiations which were concluded in Geneva under the auspices of GATT in July, 1979.
In addition, the bill contains provisions to phase out the British preferential tariff on goods imported from Great Britain and Ireland, and to withdraw it on goods from South Africa.

January 23, 1981

In order to indicate fully the importance of the implementation of the GATT agreements to Canada, I shall if I may, Mr. Speaker, give a brief outline of this institution. We may wonder what is GATT. The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, often known by its English abbreviation of GATT, refers to the multilateral treaty on trade laying down the rules of international trade and the body in Geneva which oversees compliance with the treaty and its promotion worldwide. The main objective of this treaty is to liberalize international trade and put it on a stable basis in order to contribute to the general development, growth and well-being of all the peoples of the world.
The GATT rules, Mr. Speaker, govern trade and trade relations, representing more than 80 per cent of world trade, among the 85 signatory countries. From time to time the signatories agree to undertake a round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations-MTN in short-with the ultimate objective of updating the original treaty. The last round, begun in Tokyo in 1973-and therefore known as the Tokyo Round-and completed in Geneva in June, 1979, was by far the most complex and longest of the seven negotiating rounds held since GATT was established. The general objective of the final agreement was the expansion and greater liberalization of international trade.
I would like to review briefly, Mr. Speaker, the history and background of this institution. GATT has its roots in the post-war reconstruction period. At that time, a number of countries were trying to develop a charter for the International Trade Organization or ITO, which was to have been established as a United Nations specialized agency.
However, because of the slow pace of ITO negotiations, certain countries decided to develop multilateral trade negotiations, given the name of GATT, in order to show in advance what tariff negotiations might be under the charter for the ITO. In January, 1948, nine countries, including Canada, agreed to bring the agreement into force. Since the charter for the ITO was subsequently abandoned, GATT became, by force of circumstance, the only multilateral framework for international trade. As a result, GATT has for over 30 years played the role originally intended for the ITO. After this brief review of the background of GATT, one may wonder about its importance for Canada. Since the vitality of international trade is of the utmost importance for Canada, the agreements governing international trade share in this importance.
We should not lose sight of the fact that, although Canada's domestic market is relatively small, we rank ninth among the world's trading nations. Canada stands alone among the most highly industrialized nations in lacking de facto access to a large domestic market such as is enjoyed by the United States, Japan or many members of the European Economic Community.
Customs Tariff
We can thus grasp the full importance of an agreement such as GATT which enables Canada to overcome the disadvantages inherent in its relatively small size, or in the relative concentration of its population, by giving it access to foreign markets in accordance with well-established rules. That is why Canada would have suffered a great loss today had we witnessed a strengthening of protectionism and restrictive trade practices at the last multilateral negotiations.
Now, what were Canada's objectives at the Tokyo Round negotiations? Canada, Mr. Speaker had essentially three objectives: first, to promote the development of industry, agriculture and fisheries in Canada and to increase the national income by expanding export opportunities, while ensuring an appropriate level of Canadian tariff protection. The second objective was to avoid a resurgence of protectionism and trade restrictions that adversely affect the interests of an exporting country such as ours. And the third objective, Mr. Speaker, was to improve and strengthen the international trade framework on which we depend heavily.
With these objectives in mind, let us examine the outcome of the Tokyo Round for Canada. The results of the Tokyo Round, from the Canadian point of view, show that significant progress has been made in consolidating Canada's status as a major trading nation. Besides reaching agreement on a broad package of tariff reductions averaging about 30 per cent, the negotiations took an important first step in establishing a number of agreements aimed at dismantling non-tariff barriers to trade.
Canadian tariff reductions for the vast majority of products will be phased in gradually, in such a way as to take into account the competitive position and potential of the various sectors of the Canadian economy. The effect of these reductions will be to lower the cost of the factors of production of Canadian industry, as well as the cost of a wide range of consumer goods. But let us not kid ourselves, these reductions will also challenge Canadian industry to become increasingly competitive on world markets.
The results of the negotiations are therefore of particular importance to Canada. Canada depends upon international trade for its economic well-being to a gj*eater extent than most of its trading partners. The concessions obtained in the multilateral negotiations can, if fully exploited, lead to increased production and employment in Canada. The new, expanded and more certain export opportunities that are being opened up as a result of the negotiations should bring benefits to each region of Canada and to all sectors of the economy.
In short, Mr. Speaker, in so far as trading policy is concerned, the Tokyo Round concessions should establish a solid basis for future growth in a competitive and efficient Canadian economy over the next two decades. Now, let us see how these new measures resulting from the Tokyo Round will apply to Canadian trade. As 1 have just stated, there are two important aspects to this effort to liberalize world trade, namely, the

January 23, 1981
Customs Tariff
reduction of tariff measures and the lowering of non-tariff measures. Before discussing the tariff measures we propose to include in the Customs Tariff which are covered in the bill now under study, I would like to explain briefly to the House the second aspect of the GATT agreements, namely, that of non-tariff measures.
Certain of Canada's commitments with respect to the lowering of non-tariff measures were the subject of a discussion paper which I tabled in the House on July 16, 1980, and which was referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for study on October 9 last. This paper deals with the imposition of anti-dumping and countervailing duties and emergency safeguard actions. 1 must say, Mr. Speaker, that 1 am anxious to see the work done on this paper and the standing committee report.
Second, since Canada had undertaken to revise its legislation on customs valuation, on August 29 last 1 asked the Tariff Board to initiate a review of the draft legislation and to study the impact it would have on customs duties in Canada. Third, there are certain agreements that can be brought into force in Canada without legislative change-most notably those relating to government purchasing practices and technical barriers to trade, which are also part of the non-tariff agreements we signed within the general framework of GATT.
I would like now to deal, perhaps a little longer, with tariff measures. As regards the purely tariff measures, the amendments set out in section 7(1) and schedule II of this bill would implement the tariff concessions Canada agreed to in the Tokyo Round trade negotiations. Canada approved the results of the tariff negotiations in June, 1979, and signed, subject to ratification, two GATT tariff protocols which commit participating countries to the new most favoured nation tariff rates negotiated in the Tokyo Round trade negotiations.
These protocols also set out the rules governing the phase-in of these reduced rates. They require, as a general rule, that participants reduce their tariffs in eight equal annual instalments with the Erst cut taking effect January 1, 1980. Each country negotiated a number of exceptions to this rule. For example, tariff reductions on steel will not begin until January 1, 1982, in Canada, the United States and the European Community.
Other variations were negotiated for particular products. Canada's tariff reductions are being phased in no more quickly than required by the protocols except in a few cases where there is a clear consensus in the Canadian industry for accelerated reductions. For example, the tariff reduction on computers is being implemented in five annual steps instead of the period provided for in the agreement, and that for brass band instruments is being implemented in one single step. So much so for the cornet players.
The provisions of this bill relating to the outcome of the trade negotiations are the same as those proposed by the former government in a notice of ways and means motion tabled in the House on December 12, 1979. Following the dissolution of Parliament on December 14, an order in council was passed to give interim effect to the first stage of the tariff reductions. The order was revoked when the motion was reintroduced in Parliament on June 2, 1980. In addition to implementing the agreed tariff cuts, the bill provides, in section 5, authority for the government to withdraw concessions in the event other countries should fail to fulfil their obligations under international trade agreements.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal briefly with our proposed amendments to the list of beneficiaries of the British preferential-BP-tariff. This bill also incorporates proposals made by the Conservative government for phasing out the British preferential tariff on goods from Britain and Ireland and withdrawing the British preferential tariff on goods from South Africa. It also revokes three acts of Parliament relating to the preferential trade agreements with these countries. Upon termination of the British preferential tariff treatment, imports from these countries will be subject to most-favoured-nation tariff rates.
At this point I would like to explain a bit further the phase-out schedule for the British preferential tariff. This phase-out schedule for British and Irish goods is as follows:
Where the existing British preferential rate is lower than the final most-favoured-nation concession rate-that is the rate that will apply in 1987 when all stages of the agreement will be completed-the bill proposes that the rate of duty on goods from Britain and Ireland would be increased to the MFN level in not more than three stages commencing on June 3, 1980, and ending on January 1, 1982. The result is that in many cases the rates on British and Irish goods, although higher than at present, will be lower than MFN rates until January 1, 1987, because the MFN rate reductions will be phased in gradually over the period 1980-1987. Where the BP rate is equal to or higher than the final MFN concession rate, the BP rate will remain at its current level until the MFN rate is reduced to that level.
Now, a few words concerning the measures in the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance. The tariff measures proposed in the budget of October 28, 1980, are incorporated in part IV and schedules VI to IX of the bill now under consideration. These provide duty-free entry for a range of antiques, collectables and hobby equipment as recommended by the Tariff Board in its report on reference No. 156. The Board had recommended that the current duty-free provision for such equipment be restricted to apparatus, utensils and instruments used directly in teaching or research that are not available from Canadian production. These changes will come into effect on July 1, 1981, to give eligible institutions, as well as the importers, distributors and dealers involved as well as customs officials sufficient time to adjust their administrative procedures.
Most laboratory glassware, which schools and research institutions can now import duty free, will become dutiable on July 1, 1981. Duty-free entry is also proposed for a range of goods, including plant bulbs, television captioning devices used by the deaf-this will certainly please the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who is greatly interested in these matters-as well as apparatus used to collect oyster eggs and expanded perlite, an industrial filtering agent. The bill proposes the introduction of a new tariff item to provide a single rate of duty of 15 per cent for shipments containing two or more different chemicals. This item will be used only at the request of importers and should result in reduced paperwork both for importers and the government. The bill, Mr. Speaker, also includes a number of amendments to restore tariff levels which were altered as a result of changes in tariff interpretation. The removal of authority to levy such a tax from the customs tariff means that the excise tax on imported wines will be imposed in the same manner as that on Canadian wines. In this way Canadian and imported wines will be taxed under the same legislation, that is, the Excise Tax Act.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to give a very general picture of the situation without going into the details of this bill which, as may be seen, is a sizeable and relatively technical measure, and I wanted to give the hon. members not only a general outlook but also a rather specific idea of the content of the bill.
I am very pleased that the hon. members readily recognized the importance of this bill and co-operated with their parliamentary leaders to have this bill passed promptly this afternoon. I thank the hon. members as well as the House leaders. It is therefore obvious that the passage of this bill is of paramount importance if we are to consolidate Canada's enviable position within the ranks of the world's great trading nations. I trust that the members of the standing committee will give us their support in the same manner as all members of the House were willing to co-operate, so that we may dispose of this bill promptly and efficiently in committee.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House proposes a large number of amendments to the customs tariff arising from the concessions to which Canada agreed in the last round of negotiations on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade in Geneva. As the minister pointed out, the
Customs Tariff
general objective of the final agreement was the expansion and greater liberalization of international trade.
Economic developments in Canada since the last round of negotiations on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, that is. the Kennedy Round, which was concluded in 1967, must lead any thinking person to conclude that Canada has very little to gain from a more liberalized trade policy.
Canada's unemployment rate has risen from 3.8 per cent in 1967 to 7.5 per cent in 1980. The inflation rate was 3.5 per cent in 1967 compared with 10.1 per cent in 1980. Real growth in the total output of our economy averaged over 5 per cent in the last half of the 1960s, while the real rate of growth in 1980 was .2 per cent.
In 1967 the Canadian dollar was exchanged at an 8 per cent premium over the U.S. dollar. Recently, our dollar has been discounted by over 19 per cent relative to the U.S. dollar. Canada's deficit on current account was $500 million in 1967 compared with a deficit of $137 million in 1980. These figures may lead some people to reject completely the suggestion of any further move toward a more liberalized trading agreement.
However, in my view the experience resulting from the Kennedy Round of GATT negotiations is a poor test of the potential benefits which could be derived from free trade agreements. I say this for two fundamental reasons. First, I question to what extent trade was liberalized after the Kennedy Round of negotiations. The Kennedy Round did not directly address the question of non-tariff barriers. To a large extent the lowering of tariff barriers following the Kennedy Round was counterbalanced by increases in non-tariff barriers, or what has to be called the "new protectionism". Second, even if there had been a significant degree of trade liberalization following the Kennedy Round, a country could only reap the benefits of that liberalization if the country had also undertaken a process of industrial planning geared toward a full employment strategy.
Indeed, a full employment economy is the best adjustment program conceivable in the context of approaching liberalized trade. In my view it is essential that the issue of employment must be the paramount issue in trade negotiations. I venture to say the time has come to change some of the traditional ways of looking at international trading agreements. In Canada's traditional trade structure our imports are considerably more labour intensive than our exports. Canada has been exporting our natural resources, a large part of which are non-renewable resources.
If trade balances were calculated in job terms rather than in dollar terms it would be shown clearly that our performance in international trade negotiations has been less than effective on behalf of Canada's work force. I am concerned that the dimension of jobs in international negotiations is not given the consideration it should be given by our negotiators, or by those who advise them in those trade negotiations. This government in particular has shown itself to be oblivious to the problems of
6520

unemployment and the effects it has on Canadians. I believe most Canadians would support policies or initiatives to establish national trade agreements to liberalize trade through the process of multilateral trade negotiations, such as GATT.
Having said that, Canadians want fair trade in the true sense of the word. They want to know that in the process of trading with other countries they will not end up holding the short end of the stick at every turn. Canadians are a fair-minded and realistic people who know and understand that in any set of negotiations there is a certain give and take, that you win some and you lose some. We know that and accept it, but we will not accept being on the losing end at every turn. Internationally, we have gained the reputation of being patsies in those negotiations. The relaxation of tariff barriers has been the objective of all GATT countries for decades. We know that. This government knew at the outset, when discussions began in Tokyo back in 1973, that there would be considerable pressures to reduce tariffs on a whole host of products. The government knew this and it had a fairly good idea of what it was prepared to give away in these negotiations, but it did nothing to prepare Canadian industry for what was coming.
Many of those industries, which are existing on the sole basis that their products are protected by tariffs, may now expect to suffer severe hardships and perhaps even collapse, as a result of the government's performance in these negotiations. Since then I have seen no evidence of any government measures to assist either those companies which are affected by the outcome of those negotiations, or the people who rely on the continued operation of those companies in order to earn a livelihood.
Mr. Speaker, I see no evidence that the government even recognized the effects its performance is having on the economic life of our country. I see no evidence that the government remotely recognizes that embarking on a free trade policy now will no doubt hasten the transition of our branch plant economy into that of a warehouse economy, where we will simply be a storer of goods for distribution to our domestic markets, rather than manufacturing those goods ourselves for our own security. As effective negotiators, this government fails on every count. As economic managers, this government fails on every count. As a government responsible to those it claims to govern, this government is a failure.
To bring before this House measures such as this, without also bringing forward an industrial strategy to develop an independent Canadian manufacturing base, is a sure way, at least in my view, of guaranteeing that Canada will continue to sell off our raw materials and import the finished goods we require in our country.
Perhaps I may have been a wee bit too harsh in my criticism of the government. Perhaps there is still hope. Perhaps the government has something up its sleeve which it will produce soon and not wait for the next election. Perhaps the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) was sincere and meant every word when he spoke on GATT in the House on November 5, 1979, as reported in Hansard. He said:
The process of parliamentary consideration of these changes should begin as soon as possible. As part of this process, it is absolutely essential that this government presents to the House, at the same time as it presents the measures to adopt the changes arising out of the GATT tariff negotiations, measures of adjustment assistance, measures to assist not just the industry affected by tariff changes but also the workers in that industry to cope with the effects of these changes.
Perhaps in the course of this debate the government will introduce the other measures promised and will table them in the House, perhaps by Monday next. My mind boggles at the thought.

If I may, I will refer to the comments made by the minister at the opening of his statement in the debate on this bill. Approximately $350 million is to be dedicated to employment and to an industrial strategy. The minister mentioned a larger figure, but I do not believe we have the dedication of a larger figure anywhere. What we have is support of some industries and a job-retraining program.
In the last nine months of this government there has been a decrease of approximately 43,000 manufacturing jobs. That is in the manufacturing sector alone. While there has been an increase in total jobs, these have been in a non-productive area, namely, the service sector. They have not been in the manufacturing sector. Over the long term there is no doubt this creates tremendous problems for Canada.
It would be interesting to find out what the results of those other surveys were, not just on the basis of the constitutional discussions, but also to find out what the people at large are thinking about the priorities which the government has set for its legislation and where it is putting its energies.
The second part of the priority discussion would have to deal with research and development. Of interest to everyone was the statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made on New Year's Day about the dedication which this government will have to research and development and the many opportunities it can provide to this country. I found it passing strange that it should be the Prime Minister on New Year's Day who would make a statement like that when during his tenure the dedication of finances from this government decreased from 1.25 per cent of the gross national product in 1969 to less than 0.9 per cent at the present time. I know that some additional efforts have been made lately, but efforts have been feeble in comparison to the real requirement to get back on
a sound economic basis and be competitive with countries around the world. We should not build our economy on the basis of cheap natural resources. We should not take our cheap natural resources and channel them into non-productive and inequitable systems. Rather, we should build on the basis of providing efficiency, on the basis of providing world-scale products through research and development. Through good management we should bring our products into line with what is economic for the rest of the world.
In conclusion, I think members on this side of the House are optimistic about the opportunities we have in Canada. However, we do not see priorities being taken by the government now to take advantage of these tremendous opportunities. The real needs of this country are not being taken care of; namely, energy, social development and, on the broadest scale, on the unity questions which are important to all of us.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to participate in this debate to deal with the amendments to the Income Tax Act arising out of the budget of last October. I must say the document is quite large and weighty. You would think from the size of it that it promised a great deal. It certainly promises a great deal, but I do not think it delivers much at all.
Because of the experience over the last several months since the budget was brought down, it is clear to everyone by now that the budgetary policy of the government is not working. Our economic experience since last October has been negative, disruptive to communities and to people. Present forecasts are gloomy and negative as well. Hon. members do not have to take my word for those forecasts, they come also from objective and reputable sources. For example, forecasts from the Conference Board of Canada for economic activity in 1981 indicate that we Will have poor growth, high inflation, high unemployment, and low housing starts. Obviously, we will have a continued increase in the number of bankruptcies as well. This is not a picture of an economy that is well managed. It is not the result of the actions of a compassionate or an effective government. The actions which have been undertaken so far are clearly inadequate. That is why I make reference to this weighty document which promises so much, but is delivering so little.
Not only are these policies not working in general as economic policies, they are not working specifically in terms of the programs or the specific areas of the economy they are suppose to be helping. In other words, they are not working at the general level of policy, nor at any specific level.
Although the Small Business Development Bond has been extended for a period of time through amendments to the Income Tax Act, the reason for this extension is not a newfound interest in economic activities on the part of the government, but is a result of the government's slipshod administration. When the government originally announced the introduction of Small Business Development Bonds, which were meant to help small business with the extremely high interest rates we
January 23, 1981

now have, it was very slow to make the information about them available to small business people and to the banking community. At the beginning the government simply did not get the program off the ground and now it is extending the program because of its own administrative mess. Clearly that program is not doing the job. What we really need to do is to convince the government to put its heart into this matter and to re-examine its monetary policies. This country cannot continue to throw oil on the fires of inflation. Goodness knows we are giving away all the oil we have, so why throw oil on the fire of inflation?
The Small Business Development Bond program should continue, and where it can help it will be appreciated, but it is totally inadequate as an economic policy and as a small business policy.
There are other areas which substantiate what I am saying about these policies not being effective economic policies or being effective specific programs for different sectors of the economy. For example, the amendments to the Income Tax Act contain MURBs which are really the tax write-offs and giveaways that enable large corporations to build more bachelor apartments in our cities.
What we need are measures which would lead to affordable family housing. But tax write-offs continue to allow income tax to be inequitable. In other words, people who earn high incomes are able to claim write-offs and so avoid paying their fair share. There is no guarantee MURBs will meet the housing needs which exist in the community. In fact, the program does very little for the real housing need in this country, the need of families to be well housed at affordable prices. This government's monetary policies continue to make that impossible. They do nothing about it.
Those are two simple and straightforward examples of the ineffective policies of this government. That is not the end of it; only the beginning. For example, there is the investment tax credit program with its system of write-offs and giveaways to corporations. It is another version of a previous tax write-off program for designated areas. Not only is it expensive for the public treasury, but it does not achieve the objective of assisting regional economic development in the poorer areas and creating the jobs and wealth to which we are all entitled. It is a giveaway to large corporations which can add it to their profits. They invest that money elsewhere, however, rather than in the region, which makes this program very expensive and ineffective. A new approach is needed in this area.
I want to give an example of how expensive this is. The program which this one replaces, the graduated tax credit program which graduated taxes from 7 to 20 per cent for regional development, in 1980 in the manufacturing sector cost us $170 million, and $125 million in the resource area.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: What did it produce?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is the question, what does it produce? It certainly costs a lot. Transportation and equipment cost
Income Tax Act
another $40 million and research and development, $45 million. It has done very little to encourage Canadian-owned business.
This is not a new policy. Even though it is ineffective and is clearly a giveaway, as far back as 1963, Walter Gordon, then Liberal finance minister, was acting in the very same fashion. He introduced an identical write-off measure for designated areas which cost the taxpayers great amounts of money and produced very little. Even though such policies have been followed since 1963, there are still regions of great disparities in this country. Nothing has changed. Inequities continue under the policies being pursued by the Liberal government in a non-thinking manner.
The story goes on. Again, that is not the end. The government continues with similar inequitable and ineffective policies. I want briefly to touch on some of them. In the area of corporate taxation, the level of corporate taxes which companies should pay in this country, the nominal corporate tax rate, is 46 per cent. However, the real tax rate is much lower because of various forms of write-offs.
I wish to put on record some facts and figures which come from a finance department study, and are not something 1 dreamed up. Compared with the official corporate taxation rate in this country of 46 per cent in 1977, the manufacturing sector paid 20 per cent, and oil and gas 11 per cent. I am sure it is even less than that now. According to the 1977 study, the mining sector paid 10 per cent and the banks 9 to 13 per cent. We should all own a bank. The average was 18 per cent compared with the official rate of 40 per cent.
The government has moved to extend the 5 per cent federal corporate surtax introduced last April in an attempt to rectify the situation created by a declining rate of corporate taxation. It has acknowledged the problem created by the write-offs, deductions and other forms of incentives it created, including the investment tax credit which I have already mentioned.
The government recognized the problem and took a hesitant step forward, but has not gone far enough. A 5 per cent level of taxation is not enough. We as individuals would certainly like the government to give us that kind of deal, but it is not about to do so.
I want to refer briefly to the taxation of chartered banks. This bill gives another break to the banks, which now pay a tax rate of 9 to 13 per cent. In future banks will be able to deduct from taxes, bad or doubtful debts; if a bank makes a bad business deal, it may deduct the amount involved from its taxes. This can now be done during the year it appears on their books. However, with the change, they can defer this deduction, carrying it over from year to year. This is an additional benefit to them. In addition to increasing their profits, they may now profit from business failures. Imagine the possibility of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce profiting from the failure of Massey-Ferguson. That is economic insanity and stupidity which boggles the mind.
I come back to the question of regional development and the need for economic development in the less-developed areas.

January 23, 1981
Income Tax Act
Earlier I referred to the ineffectiveness of the investment tax credit and the fact that it does not do anything for the poorer areas of this country. With the set of amendments in this heavy document, the government is doing something about regional disparities and regional economic activity. 1 come now to the provisions with regard to marginal manufacturing. The 9 per cent federal sales tax on marginal manufacturing is being expanded and will include assembling, mixing, cutting to size or packaging when done other than in a retail store for sale to customers. This is supposedly being done to overcome inequities. The real impact of this measure is that it extends the federal sales tax to a sector of small business which has a high bankruptcy rate and, therefore, can least afford it.
I received a letter from a firm in Manitoba detailing the inequities and injustices of the extension of this tax. It points out that this measure will call for additional record-keeping by small businessmen. If there is one message that small business people across this nation have consistently been delivering to governments over the years, it is to cut out all unnecessary red tape and paperwork imposed on small business. As I said, this measure will increase it.
This tends to put small businesses in a non-competitive position with companies which import prepackaged products. In other words, it makes things more difficult for the company which packages materials, in this case in Winnipeg, Manitoba, than for the company which imports materials already packaged. That is a clear injustice which will increase unemployment and encourage us to export jobs. It also tends to centralize packaging within our own domestic market in Canada. In other words, it would tend to be advantageous to do packaging in industrial Canada, in Ontario and Quebec, and it would be disadvantageous to do packaging in a region like Winnipeg which has slow economic activity at this point. I think that is directly contrary to the government's policies of sound regional economic equity.
Clearly we should not be introducing a measure that is going to export jobs and shift jobs from slow-growth regions to the industrial heartland. I have a concern about industry in Ontario and Quebec. My party has long and well spoken of the need for an industrial strategy in our country. That is the way to keep Ontario healthy and keep jobs here. But let us not rob Manitoba of jobs for Ontario. That clearly is injustice carried to the extreme. I am glad businessmen from Manitoba took the trouble to write me.
What we are dealing with today are amendments to the Income Tax Act arising out of a budget. One of the things about the Income Tax Act is that it is progressive, at least that is what we have always been led to believe. It is a means to promote equity and justice in the country in terms of the distribution of income. I want to talk a bit about the distribution of income and the impact of these amendments on that distribution. Clearly, from what I have said up until now, the impact of these measures is to promote inequity, to give gifts to the rich and to destroy the progressiveness of our taxation
system. In other words, those who have the most will pay their fair share-will pay the most-and those who have the least will pay what they can afford-pay the least. I want to talk a little bit about income distribution.
Let me draw to your mind and attention to the book "The Canadian Fact Book On Income Distribution". This is a book I find very enlightening and one which I have been careful to read, particularly after hearing about the concern in this House for the incomes and pensions of such people as judges and others in that category.
This book gives the picture of income distribution in this country. We have the bottom fifth of the population earning roughly 4 per cent of the wealth with the top fifth earning something like 40 per cent of the wealth. Can you imagine that the poorest people in this country earn one tenth of what those with the top incomes earn, while those at the top of the heap earn ten times as much as those at the bottom? What kind of income distribution is that and why should we continue to promote that kind of distribution through the Income Tax Act, and in fact make it worse? That is what concerns me.
The level of distribution of income in this country has been steady since 1951 according to this study, which appears to me to be a sound and good study. Clearly, after the world depression and the years of the 1930s we took a step forward. We introduced social welfare measures and we introduced an income floor.
I am not challenging the idea or the notion that we have redistribution of income in this country. We do. We have a floor and this study demonstrates that the people earning the least do benefit from the transfer of payments we make in this country. That is well'and good. What I am pointing out now is that the disparities of the distribution of income in this country have not changed significantly since 1951 and this shows we have not moved toward a more just and equitable society since 1951. That is sad when you consider that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came in on a wave of hope that we could have a just society. He has failed dismally to fulfil that hope and he continues today to play Liberal politics by introducing, in effect, unjust taxation measures.
Let me quote from this study with regard to taxes as paid by the rich and the poor in this country. At page 52 in a statement relating to the distribution of income after all taxes, it states that in a study for the Royal Commission on Taxation in the 1960s it was first demonstrated that the over-all tax system is not progressive, and in fact it taxes the poor very heavily.
A little further down the page it is stated:
-the bottom income class still pays the highest rate of taxation.

They still do and that is shocking. It is not necessary in a country such as ours. It certainly should not be allowed to continue and we should not be promoting it. That is what is being done with these measures, I suggest, and it is being done in the name of income management, an income

management which has been demonstrated by our own personal experience in this country since last October to be ineffective. It really has no final justification.
Let me touch briefly on the energy program. In my view the energy program of the government is a sham. I do not want to go into detail about it because I know my colleague, our energy critic, has dealt with the program adequately. I mention it because there are measures in this bill in relation to the program. It is a sham. They call it Canadianization, but in fact it is continued control by multinational corporations. Our energy critic labelled it "Lalondization". 1 take him to mean by that a Liberal trick, rhetoric without action, sleight of hand without substance.

Let me touch upon pricing of oil as outlined in this program. The Liberal government, like the Tory government when it was in office, is moving toward a price equal to 85 per cent of the world price. That is clear from both budgetary documents. This is the fact on the Tory side in spite of its proposed tax credit on oil, even taking that into account the pricing policy remains similar, by and large. The approach to the pricing of the product is the same. I must say 1 feel we need an energy policy on pricing that will result in justifiable prices. We need an oil price review commission. Price increases must be reviewed in public.
1 would make the same suggestion with respect to oil. The base of our activity must be a public corporation. The simplest way I can illustrate that for you, Mr. Speaker, is to use the example of Autopac in Manitoba. It is a public corporation that offers auto insurance at a price related to the cost of delivering the service.
The people of Manitoba clearly understand this because they have experience with Autopac, and 1 suggest that the same rationale for a public corporation exists in the energy sector as exists in the car insurance sector. One of the things such a corporation would do is keep the energy dollars each of us pays every day for heating our homes and driving our cars, in an energy account. It would not let any government siphon off those dollars for any other purpose, and it would not allow multinational corporations to siphon them off for their own profit or investment in land deals or any other investment in which they might be interested. I know that the energy program illustrated in these amendments is inadequate and a sham and allows continued control by multinational corpora-

I want to move back again to the budgetary policies which are illustrated and reflected in this document and which came out with the budget. I will mention some things which I think are missing.
It is clear now that we have a recession in this country. The only distinction about this recession is that we also have a very high rate of inflation with it. That is the only distinctive achievement of the economic policy of the government across the way. With the recessionary situation we are in now we really need public investment to stimulate and get the economy moving again, to provide jobs and to create wealth. By creating wealth we create a source for taxes in order to get the deficit down.

Let me illustrate the need for investment. I suggest that a good place to invest would be in the area of urban transit. We clearly must do something about energy conservation. The government has an energy program. Let us invest adequately in mass urban transit. This would create jobs. If we develop transit systems in this country, we can sell them not only to our own cities but also to American and European cities.
We can create high technology jobs in this country through investment in mass transit. We could conserve energy by doing that. We could promote a better living environment in the cities, where most of our citizens now live. We could provide a convenient method for people to go to work in cities. I think that is important. We need public investment now which, as it works its way through the economy, would create wealth, and that investment should be in urban transit.
I mention this specifically today because toward the need of next week there will be a national conference in Winnipeg which representatives from cities across the country will attend. The theme of that conference will be energy and urban transit. Let us send a signal from here that this government is concerned about energy, about urban transit and about the economy. This should be in the budgetary policy of the government, but it is not.
Since we are dealing with an income tax bill, I point out that action is needed in other areas as well. For example, there should be changes in the Income Tax Act to promote the rehabilitation and preservation of heritage buildings. I am very familiar with this subject because I have served on the city council in Winnipeg and worked in the designation of heritage buildings. This is a subject which is close to my heart. Present income tax laws encourage the demolition of heritage build-

January 23, 1981
Income Tax Act
ings rather than their rehabilitation. There must be changes in the Income Tax Act soon so that we can promote a positive effect on the shape and nature of our cities. We do not want to live in cities made up simply of steel structures which do not reflect the history and experience of our people. We must promote the rehabilitation of our heritage buildings so that when we live, walk, play and work in our cities we can have a sense of the experience of our people and a sense of our history.
However, changes in the Income Tax Act in this respect would achieve not just those goals only, but would also promote employment. Rehabilitation is job intensive. Rehabilitation would create a whole new industry.
This is not just another airy-fairy idea. It is not pie in the sky. It is not impossible. I have with me today a number of studies. I also have specific proposals for amendments to the Income Tax Act. These proposals are from Heritage Winnipeg, and I will be raising them again in this House at the earliest opportunity. These studies examined the American experience and demonstrated that what I am calling for has been done. It has not been done in some far-away nation upon whose approach we might cast some doubt but by our closest neighbour, the United States.
These studies of federal tax changes in the United States show that a system of saving heritage structures can work. Employment, wealth and economic activity can be generated by this kind of activity. The tax laws we presently have encourage demolition and leave our cities as dead places where there is nothing of value from the past. We are a young country, and it is a good time now to start to preserve our history for today's generation as well as tomorrow's. I will be raising this issue again in this House. I just want to flag it now to let the government know that I will be pursuing it and urging the government to act on it in a positive way.
This government has some good policies. One of these policies is followed by the Department of Public Works. Parks Canada has a responsibility for heritage in this country. It is my understanding that there is a policy which encourages Parks Canada to locate heritage buildings in cities across the country. That is a good, positive policy. However, in Winnipeg today this policy is being administered poorly. The Department of Public Works and Parks Canada propose to move into a marginally historic structure in Winnipeg rather than into a first-rate, top-notch historic building.
If Parks Canada were to move into that first-rate, top-notch historic building, it could be preserved for generations to come. Instead, just because the government presently owns a marginally historic building, it will not move into the first-class building and preserve something which is of real value. That is poor administration. When a government goes so far as to establish a good policy, it should follow it up with good administration.
1 will conclude. I just want to say I am glad I had this opportunity to participate in this debate. I think that we must conclude that the changes to the Income Tax Act are just not good enough and go in the wrong direction. We need an
economic program, an economic policy, economic management in this country. We need a tax policy which works toward the specific objectives for which it is intended; one which promotes economic activity, which is equitable and just, which promotes a fair distribution of income in the country, and which also deals with the problem that is on the minds of people in Canada today, a policy which deals effectively in the area of energy. So let members on the other side of the House wake up, face up to the real problems of this country and get moving.
